title: Psalm 143: No One Alive Is Righteous Before You
summary: David asks the LORD to hear his plea on the basis of God's own faithfulness and righteousness, not his own, since no living person is righteous before God. Crushed by an enemy and sitting in darkness, he remembers God's past works, stretches out his hands like parched land, and asks to hear of God's loving devotion in the morning. He asks to be taught to do God's will and led by God's good Spirit on level ground.
story: Psalm 143 is the last of four prayers for rescue (Psalms 140 to 143) in the Psalter's final Davidic collection. It gathers up their themes (enemies, traps, a faint spirit, a plea for refuge) and adds something new: a confession that the psalmist has no righteousness of his own to plead. Where Psalm 142 ended in a cave, Psalm 143 ends with the psalmist asking to be taught and led. It is followed by Psalm 144, a royal psalm of victory, and Psalm 145, the Psalter's last psalm of David, so the long cry for help in 140 to 143 gives way to praise.
historical:
The heading reads “A Psalm of David.” As with other headings, it may identify the author or record the psalm's place in a Davidic collection, and scholars differ. The Septuagint adds a note connecting the psalm with the time when David's son pursued him, which would place it during Absalom's revolt (2 Samuel 15 to 18), but that note is not in the Hebrew text. The psalm itself describes an enemy who has crushed the psalmist's life to the ground and made him dwell in darkness like the dead, language general enough to fit many situations of persecution or illness.

Christian tradition since at least the sixth century has counted Psalm 143 as the last of the seven penitential psalms (Psalms 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, and 143), a group used especially during Lent for confession and repentance. Psalm 143 is not primarily a confession of a specific sin, but its admission in verse 2 that no one alive is righteous before God made it a natural fit.
cultural:
The image of stretching out the hands to God (verse 6) was the ordinary posture of prayer in Israel, palms open and raised. The comparison with a parched land draws on the climate of the region, where the long dry summer left the ground cracked and thirsty until the autumn rains. Morning (verse 8) was associated with deliverance and fresh mercy; many psalms describe God's help arriving at dawn after a night of distress (Psalm 30:5 and 46:5).

The Pit (verse 7) is another name for the grave or Sheol, the realm of the dead. To be like those who go down to the Pit was to be as good as dead. Level ground (verse 10) was a highly valued image in hill country, where roads were rough and steep; a level path meant safety and ease of travel, and it became a common picture for a life lived in God's ways.
literary: Psalm 143 is an individual lament in two halves, each ending with Selah or a request. Verses 1 to 6 describe the psalmist's plea and distress, moving from an appeal to God's faithfulness (verses 1 and 2), to the enemy's attack (verses 3 and 4), to memory and longing (verses 5 and 6). Verses 7 to 12 are a series of urgent requests: answer me quickly, let me hear, teach me, deliver me, lead me, revive me, cut off my enemies. The psalm begins and ends with God's righteousness (verses 1 and 11) and with the psalmist as God's servant (verses 2 and 12), a frame that shows the psalmist's hope rests entirely on God's character.

outline.t: Hear me in your faithfulness, not my righteousness
Crushed by the enemy, faint in spirit
Remembering God's works, thirsting for him
Answer me, teach me, lead me
Revive me for your name's sake

doctrines.note: The psalmist does not appeal to his own righteousness but to God's. No one alive is righteous before God, so rescue must rest on God's faithfulness and loving devotion. This is the Old Testament root of the gospel's teaching that salvation is by grace.

The psalmist asks God's good Spirit to lead him on level ground. The Old Testament speaks of God's Spirit guiding and instructing his people (Nehemiah 9:20), anticipating the fuller New Testament teaching on the Spirit's work in believers.

Verse 2 states the universal reality of human sin: no one alive is righteous before God. The psalmist does not deny his guilt; he asks God not to enter into judgment with him, but to act out of mercy.

words.note: Tsadaq, to be righteous or to be justified. The verb can mean to be in the right, especially in a legal case. Verse 2 says that no one alive will be justified before God if he enters into judgment with them. Paul echoes this verse when he writes that no one will be justified by works of the law (Romans 3:20 and Galatians 2:16).

Tsedaqah, righteousness. In the Psalms, God's righteousness is often his faithfulness to act rightly, especially to save his people and uphold justice. Verses 1 and 11 appeal to God's righteousness as the basis for rescue. It is not only a standard that condemns but a saving power on which the psalmist can rely.

Ruach, spirit, breath, or wind. In verse 4 it describes the psalmist's own spirit growing faint, and in verse 7 his spirit failing. In verse 10 it names God's good Spirit, who leads. The psalm moves from a failing human spirit to the guiding divine Spirit.

christ: Paul draws on verse 2 when he argues that no human being will be justified in God's sight by works of the law (Romans 3:20 and Galatians 2:16). The psalmist, knowing he cannot stand before God on his own merit, appeals to God's faithfulness and righteousness, and the New Testament proclaims that God's righteousness has been revealed in Christ, who justifies the ungodly through faith (Romans 3:21-26). The psalm's request for God's good Spirit to lead finds its answer in the gift of the Spirit to all who belong to Christ (Romans 8:14). The psalmist's plea not to be judged by his own righteousness is exactly the plea the gospel answers: God has provided a righteousness that is not our own. The connection is not a prediction but a principle, taken up and fulfilled in the gospel.
questions: The psalmist appeals to God's righteousness, not his own. What difference does it make to approach God on that basis?
Verse 5 describes remembering God's past works in a time of darkness. What past acts of God could you remember when you feel crushed?
The psalmist asks to be taught to do God's will. Is that a prayer you find easy or hard to pray, and why?
